belief: If I leave my culture behind, I'm betraying my people.
origins: Those who move for education, work, marriage, or faith can feel torn. Family may say, “You think you’re better than us,” or hint that adopting new ways is disloyal. We can feel guilt about changing language, food, customs, or beliefs, as if growth were abandonment.
teaches: Scripture honors peoples and cultures: “From one man He made every nation of men,” and John sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue” before the throne. Ruth left her homeland and told Naomi, “Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God,” and was honored. Paul writes that in Christ “there is no Greek or Jew… but Christ is all and is in all.” We can honor our heritage, keep what is good, and still follow Christ where His way differs from our culture’s. Changing does not mean betraying, and loving where we come from does not mean staying exactly the same.
self_statements: If I change, I am abandoning them.
They will think I am better than them.
I owe them my loyalty in everything.
Growing up means leaving them behind.
I am a traitor if I adopt other ways.
I cannot belong to two worlds.
errors: Believing I must keep everything or lose everything.
Assuming my people think I am a traitor.
Feeling guilty and concluding that I did something wrong.
Insisting that I must never change.
questions: What parts of my culture do I treasure and want to keep?
What parts of my culture conflict with my faith or conscience?
What has changed, and was it a betrayal or growth?
How can I express honor to my people in a new setting?
What does Scripture say about every nation worshiping together?
Who could I talk with who has navigated two cultures?
truth: I can honor my culture and my people while following Christ and growing. Not every change is betrayal. I can keep what is good, set aside what conflicts with God’s way, and be a bridge.
hw_truths: Ruth was honored for following God.
I can honor my roots and grow.
log: Each week, note one way you honored your culture and one way you grew.
actions: Write the parts of your culture you want to keep.
Write what you cannot keep and why.
Call, visit, or share food or stories.
Talk to someone who lives between two cultures.
prayer: Lord, You made every people. Help me honor where I come from and follow You wherever You lead. Give me grace with those who worry I am leaving them. Amen.
hw_questions: How can I honor my people?
What do I need to say?
name_example: Sarah can write: “Every nation will worship together, so honoring my roots and following Christ fit together.”
